claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin iron oxide/hydroxide surface layer.
The native oxide/hydroxide layer acts as a protective barrier that suppresses corrosion at room temperature.
Elevated temperature thermally destabilizes the native film.
Enhanced film solubility and micro-cracking contribute to thermal destabilization.
Loss of film integrity at elevated temperature produces accelerated localized corrosion.
As-received Q235 steel retains an oxide/hydroxide film formed during standard processing and storage.
An intact passive film resists ingress of chloride ions and oxygen at room temperature.
Resistance to corrosive-species ingress inhibits the electrochemical reactions that drive corrosion.
Elevated temperature can cause dissolution, micro-cracking, or delamination of the native film.
Film dissolution, micro-cracking, or delamination exposes the underlying steel and accelerates corrosion.
At approximately 25 °C, film-intact Q235 steel will have significantly lower corrosion rates than film-removed steel.
At room temperature, film-intact samples will exhibit lower mass loss, higher EIS impedance, and less pitting than film-removed samples.
At approximately 70 °C, the protective effect of the native film will diminish.
Elevated-temperature samples will exhibit increased mass loss, more aggressive pitting, more negative corrosion potentials, and lower film integrity.
Processing history, steel batch, and alloying-element variations can alter native-film behavior.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome calls bare or film-removed steel the 'untreated' reference, whereas the baseline and initial-state fields define untreated or pre-exposure Q235 as retaining its native oxide film. Mechanical film removal is itself a treatment.
